newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Grain talks end amid fear of volatility.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Grain talks end amid fear of volatility.

text.p: Grain nations ended London talks on Friday with a forecast that a combination of strong demand, low food stocks and the prospect of an El Nino weather "effect" in Australia threatens volatility in the world price of wheat.
The prediction, voiced notably by Australia, was bad news for cash-strapped Third World buyers.

"I am returning home a lot more worried than when I came. Increased volatility puts buyers into the hands of exporters," a North African grain official said at the end of an annual meeting of the 44-nation International Grains Council.

Australian Wheat Board chairman Trevor Flugge earlier had predicted that world wheat demand may outstrip supply in 1997/98. He said that this would lead to a sharp, new drawdown in stocks, notably those held by major exporters like Canada and the European Union.

Flugge also said export availability from the five major exporters - the United States, Canada, the European Union, Argentina and Australia - may be down by around five to seven million tonnes of wheat.

For Australia alone Flugge predicted a crop of up to a fairly robust 20 million tonnes but gave a warning that a dry weather phenomenon arising from a forecasted warm El Nino Pacific Ocean current might spell "considerable downside".
"We believe there will be a stronger increase in import demand in 1997/98 and a more substantial fall in world stocks than is currently predicted by others in the market place," he said.
Flugge added: "As we rely more and more on actual
production of each season, rather than the level of stocks to determine market prices, I believe we will witness an increase in the level of volatility in the international market".
The AWB expects world demand for wheat to rise by some three to six million tonnes in 1997/98 with most of the rise coming from Iran, Iraq, Pakistan, India and Turkey.
Drought in Africa will also lead to increased import requirements while demand in Indonesia, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh will also rise.
AWB expects a fall in world wheat stocks of up to six million tonnes while the IGC puts the decline at three million tonnes.
World wheat prices at just under $3.50 per bushel are now well below record levels of a year ago - when they went as high as $7.50 on news that stocks had fallen to 20-year lows.
But weaker prices have so far failed to spark a major buying spree from importers, who were waiting for prices to fall further.
In the short-term buyers must respond to increased volatility by avoiding to all come out at the same time, a buyer said.

But in the longer-term they must strive to expand production and move towards self-reliance, he added. Most buyers, notably North African countries, hit by drought and poor crops at home, are expected to start seriously shopping for wheat in July when the European Union will resume grain exports. But some importers are already testing the market.
This wek Algeria bought 150,000 tonnes of Canadian wheat while Pakistan is seeking 500,000 tonnes of wheat for July-August shipment.
